sections.title: Lesson 3.1: Characteristics of Bonds
sections.overview: Bonds are debt securities representing a loan from investor to issuer (corporations, federal government, agencies, or municipalities). Investors must understand par value, maturities, coupons, pricing conventions, the inverse relationship between bond prices and interest rates, the various yield measurements, common bond features (call, put, convert), credit ratings, volatility (duration), and the benefits/risks of bond ownership.
key_concepts: Par value (face/principal): standardly $1,000 per bond; amount repaid at maturity.

Maturity types: Term (entire principal at once; may use sinking fund), Serial (principal matures in portions over time), Balloon (combines serial payments with large final maturity payment). Series bonds refer to savings bonds, not a maturity structure.
Coupon rate = nominal yield = stated yield; fixed percentage of par paid as interest (typically semiannually).

Accrued interest: buyer pays seller interest earned since last coupon. Corporate and municipal bonds use 30-day month / 360-day year. Treasury notes/bonds use actual days/actual days. Zero-coupon bonds pay no accrued interest.
Pricing in points: 1 point = 1% of par = $10. Bond quoted at 90 = $900; quoted at 103 = $1,030.
Trading levels: par ($1,000), premium (above par), discount (below par).
Inverse relationship: bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.

Yields: Nominal (coupon, fixed), Current Yield (annual coupon ÷ market price), Yield to Maturity (annualized total return if held to maturity, including discount/premium amortization), Yield to Call (return if called early).
Yield relationships at a DISCOUNT: Nominal < CY < YTM < YTC.
Yield relationships at a PREMIUM: YTC < YTM < CY < Nominal.
Yield relationships at PAR: all yields are equal.
Basis point = 1/100 of 1%; 'trading on a basis of' refers to YTM.
Call feature: benefits issuer (called when rates fall); requires higher coupon to attract investors.
Put feature: benefits investor (put back when rates rise); allows lower coupon.
Convertible feature: corporate bonds convertible into common stock; benefits investor; bond at 'parity' when bond value = value of underlying convertible shares.

Zero-coupon bonds (ZR): issued at deep discount, mature at par; no periodic interest; more volatile than comparable coupon bonds. Treasury STRIPS are Treasury-issued zeros; Treasury Receipts are dealer-created from baskets of Treasuries (NOT backed by U.S. government).
Phantom income: zero-coupon bondholders pay tax annually on accreted (imputed) interest despite no cash received.
Credit rating agencies (NRSROs): Standard & Poor's, Moody's, Fitch (A.M. Best rates insurance issues).
Investment-grade ratings: S&P AAA/AA/A/BBB; Moody's Aaa/Aa/A/Baa.
Speculative/high-yield (junk) ratings: BB/Ba and below.
Volatility: longer maturity = more volatile; lower coupon = more volatile.
Duration: measure combining maturity and coupon to gauge price volatility to interest-rate change; higher duration = more volatile.
Benefits of bonds: steady income, senior to equity in liquidation, less price volatility than stocks.
Risks: default/credit risk, interest rate risk, purchasing power (inflation) risk, call risk, reinvestment risk.
rules: Settlement (CURRENT): Corporate bonds settle T+1 (per SEC Rule 15c6-1 amendment effective 5/28/2024). Accrual convention 30/360 unchanged.
SEC-recognized NRSROs include S&P, Moody's, and Fitch.
Savings bonds, although debt of the U.S. government, do not trade in the secondary market and are exempt from many securities laws.
formulas: Annual Coupon Income = Coupon Rate × Par Value (e.g., 6% × $1,000 = $60/year)
Current Yield (CY) = Annual Coupon Payment ÷ Market Price
Bond Price in Dollars = Quoted Price × 10 (e.g., quote of 95 = $950)
1 Point = 1% of par = $10 ; 1 Basis Point = 1/100 of 1% = 0.01%
At Discount: Nominal < CY < YTM < YTC
At Premium: YTC < YTM < CY < Nominal
At Par: Nominal = CY = YTM = YTC
mnemonics: 'DIPN ↔ PYNE': at Discount, yields ascend Nominal→CY→YTM→YTC; at Premium, yields descend (flip the order).
Call = issuer's Choice; Put = investor's Power.
Issuer-friendly features (Call) = Higher coupon; Investor-friendly features (Put, Convert) = Lower coupon.
'Bills, Notes, Bonds — Buy at Discount, No Coupon, Be Patient' (T-bills only) for identifying zero-style Treasuries.
Volatility drivers: 'Long & Low' — Long maturity + Low coupon = high volatility.

sections.title: Lesson 3.1 (cont.): Corporate Bonds and Order of Liquidation
sections.overview: Corporate debt may be secured (backed by specific assets) or unsecured (backed only by issuer's credit). When a corporation fails, the bankruptcy court liquidates assets and pays claims according to a strict statutory priority order — secured creditors first, common stockholders last.
key_concepts: SECURED corporate debt: Mortgage bonds (backed by real estate), Equipment trust certificates (backed by equipment, often railroad/airline rolling stock, title held by trustee), Collateral trust bonds (backed by securities deposited in trust — must be marketable).

UNSECURED corporate debt: Debentures (backed only by issuer's full faith/credit), Guaranteed bonds (backed by a third party such as a parent company — still unsecured), Income/adjustment bonds (pay interest ONLY if BOD declares; used by companies in reorganization — NOT suitable for income-seekers), Subordinated debentures (junior to other unsecured debt).
All debt is senior to all equity.

Order of liquidation: (1) Secured debt holders, (2) Administrative claimants (attorneys, court costs, liquidators), (3) Unsecured debt holders and general creditors (including wages and taxes), (4) Subordinated debt holders, (5) Preferred stockholders, (6) Common stockholders.
Courts may shift priority of wages/taxes upward if needed.
rules: Accrued interest on corporate bonds calculated on 30-day month / 360-day year basis.
formulas: Accrued Interest (Corp/Muni) = Par × Coupon Rate × (Days from last coupon to settlement using 30/360) ÷ 360
mnemonics: Liquidation order: 'Secured Admins Use Subordinated Preferred Common' = Secured → Administrative → Unsecured/General creditors → Subordinated → Preferred → Common.
'Income bonds give NO income guarantee' — never recommend for income.

sections.title: Lesson 3.2: Government-Issued Bonds (Municipal, Treasury, and Agency)
sections.overview: This lesson covers debt issued by governmental entities: municipal securities (state/local, generally tax-advantaged), direct U.S. Treasury obligations (T-bills, T-notes, T-bonds, TIPS, STRIPS), and agency securities (FNMA, FHLMC, GNMA, FCS). Investors must master tax treatment, settlement, and structural differences.
key_concepts: MUNICIPAL BONDS: issued by states, local governments, U.S. territories, authorities, special districts.

Federal tax treatment: most muni interest is federally tax-exempt; capital gains remain taxable. State tax: exempt if investor resides in state of issuance. U.S. territory bonds (Guam, USVI, PR) are 'triple tax-exempt' — federal, state, AND local.

General Obligation (GO) bonds: backed by full faith, credit, and taxing power of issuer; finance non-revenue-producing public projects; typically require voter approval; subject to statutory debt limits. State GO backed by income/sales tax; local GO backed by ad valorem (property) taxes.
Revenue bonds: self-supporting; backed by revenues from specific facility (toll roads, airports, hospitals, utilities, stadiums); no voter approval needed; not subject to statutory debt limits.

Short-term municipal notes: TANs (tax anticipation), RANs (revenue anticipation), TRANs (tax & revenue), BANs (bond anticipation), CLNs (construction loan), GANs (grant anticipation), VRDNs (variable rate demand — with put feature), tax-exempt commercial paper (typically ≤270 days).
TREASURY SECURITIES — backed by full faith and credit of U.S. government; book-entry only; settle T+1.
T-Bills: ≤52 weeks; issued at discount, mature at par; no stated coupon; the 13-week T-bill is the benchmark 'risk-free' rate.
T-Notes: 2–10 year maturities; semiannual interest; priced as % of par.
T-Bonds: >10–30 year maturities; semiannual interest; priced as % of par.
TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities): 5, 10, or 20-year maturities; fixed coupon; principal adjusted semiannually for inflation/deflation; final principal never below original par.
Treasury STRIPS: zero-coupon Treasuries; backed by U.S. government; created via Treasury's stripping program.
Treasury Receipts: zero-coupon products created by broker-dealers from a basket of Treasuries; NOT backed by full faith and credit of U.S. government.
Accrued interest on Treasury notes/bonds: actual days / actual days.
AGENCY SECURITIES: GNMA (Ginnie Mae) — only agency fully backed by U.S. government; FNMA (Fannie Mae) and FHLMC (Freddie Mac) — publicly-held GSEs; SLMA (Sallie Mae); FCS (Farm Credit System).
GNMA pass-throughs pay monthly principal + interest; subject to prepayment risk.
Agency MBS settle T+1 under current SEC 15c6-1 amendments (specific TBA mortgage trades follow separate SIFMA schedules).
Tax-equivalent yield: used to compare a tax-exempt municipal yield to a fully-taxable yield.
rules: Municipal bond settlement: T+1 (MSRB Rules G-12 and G-15 amended effective 5/28/2024 — MSRB Notice 2023-19).
Agency security settlement: generally T+1 under current rules.
Municipal interest: federally tax-exempt; state-tax-exempt if resident; territory bonds tax-exempt at all levels.
Treasury interest: federally taxable; exempt from state and local taxes.
formulas: Tax-Equivalent Yield = Tax-Free (Muni) Yield ÷ (100% − Investor's Marginal Tax Rate)
Municipal-Equivalent Yield = Corporate (Taxable) Yield × (100% − Investor's Marginal Tax Rate)
After-Tax Yield (taxable bond) = Taxable Yield × (1 − Tax Rate)
mnemonics: 'GO = Government's Obligation' (taxes); 'Revenue = Revenue from the project'.
'Ginnie is the Government's' — only GNMA has full U.S. backing among agencies.
Treasury terms by length: 'BILLS short, NOTES middle, BONDS long' (≤1 yr / 2–10 yr / >10–30 yr).
TANs/RANs/BANs/CLNs/GANs — 'short-term munis are all ANs (Anticipation Notes)'.

sections.title: Lesson 3.3: Money Market and Asset-Backed Securities
sections.overview: Money market instruments are short-term (≤1 year), highly liquid, low-yield debt used for cash management. Asset-backed securities (ABS), including CMOs and CDOs, are created by pooling and securitizing underlying assets into tranches with varying risk and maturity profiles. This lesson also summarizes bond interest taxation across issuer types.
key_concepts: Money market securities: maturities ≤1 year; highly liquid; generally very safe; low return; usually issued at a discount (jumbo CDs are an exception — pay interest).
Jumbo (negotiable) CDs: ≥$100,000 face (often $1M+); fixed rate; tradable in secondary market; FDIC insurance is capped at $250,000 per depositor per insured bank per ownership category.
Bankers' Acceptances (BAs): time draft used in import/export trade; max 270 days (typically 1–180); issued at discount.
Commercial paper: unsecured corporate promissory notes; 1–270 days (most ≤90); issued at discount; high-credit issuers only.
T-Bills: covered as both Treasury and money market instrument.
T-notes/T-bonds become money market instruments when ≤1 year remains to maturity.
Repurchase agreements (Repos): seller of securities agrees to repurchase later at higher price; used by banks/dealers/Fed for short-term financing.
Reverse Repos: dealer buys securities with agreement to resell later.
Federal Funds: overnight loans between member banks of excess reserves; the fed funds rate is set by the market.
SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate): the USD reference rate that replaced LIBOR, which was permanently discontinued 6/30/2023. Floating-rate notes and many derivatives now reference SOFR.
Money market suitability: appropriate for short-term cash needs, liquidity, safety — NOT suitable for long-term growth or income because of low and fluctuating yields and reinvestment risk.
ASSET-BACKED SECURITIES (ABS): pool of loans/receivables securitized into investable tranches; diversifies risk; settles T+1 under current rules.

Collateralized Mortgage Obligations (CMOs): pool of residential mortgages organized into tranches; each tranche receives principal sequentially (one tranche at a time); interest paid to all tranches monthly; subject to prepayment risk (faster payoffs when rates fall) and extension risk (slower payoffs when rates rise); principal repaid in $1,000 increments to randomly selected bonds within a tranche; often backed by GNMA/FNMA/FHLMC pass-throughs.
Collateralized Debt Obligations (CDOs): pools of NON-mortgage debt (corporate bonds, auto loans, leases, credit card receivables, derivatives); structured into tranches with varying risk/return.

BOND INTEREST TAXATION SUMMARY: Treasury — federally taxable, state/local exempt; Municipal — federal exempt, state depends on residency; FNMA/FHLMC — fully taxable (federal + state/local); GNMA — fully taxable (federal + state/local), pays monthly; U.S. territory bonds — exempt at all levels.
rules: ABS and similar securities settle T+1 under amended SEC Rule 15c6-1 (effective 5/28/2024).
LIBOR permanently discontinued 6/30/2023 — replaced by SOFR for USD reference rates.
FDIC insurance limit: $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category.
formulas: Discount-Basis Yield (T-bill style) = [(Face − Purchase Price) ÷ Face] × (360 ÷ Days to Maturity)
Approximate Yield on Discount Money Market Instrument = (Discount ÷ Purchase Price) × (365 ÷ Days to Maturity)
mnemonics: Money market = 'Short, Safe, Sub-par yield' (the 3 S's).
CMO = 'C for Collateralized, M for Mortgage' — only mortgages.
CDO = 'C for Collateralized, D for Debt (non-mortgage)'.
Taxation: 'Treasury = Federal only; Muni = State possible; Agency = All taxable (except GNMA full faith but still fully taxed)'.
'GNMA pays Gradually Monthly' — monthly P&I distributions.
